newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Jan real ind output contracts +3.9 pct yr/yr.
newsitem.headline: Czech Jan real ind output contracts +3.9 pct yr/yr.

text.p: Czech real final industrial production in January contracted by 3.9 percent, year-on-year, after a 12.0 percent rise in the same month of the previous year, the Statistical Bureau (CSU) said on Wednesday.
It added that average industrial monthly wages grew, in nominal terms, 14.4 percent in January compared with a 21.1 percent rise in December, year-on-year.
The CSU also said that real construction output for January contracted by 18.6 percent, year-on-year.
The CSU added that industrial sales for January, in real terms, eased by 0.2 percent, year-on-year.

NOTE. The CSU said in a statement that it had changed its methodology for calculating industrial production. The new methodology excludes multiple calculation of semi-finished products, resources, and other materials and commodities, which were included in output data at every stage under the old method measuring the gross value of all goods produced.
The new index measures output changes by units, weight or other measurements, of the total of 1,304 products out of 879 product groups consisting of one or more similar products.

The product groups's output indices are placed in sectors, using weighting equal to their weight in the respective industrial sector. The overall index is calculated from weighted changes in the sectoral indices.

The CSU said that the fall of industrial production was influenced by raw materials production such as coal and other minerals and in the category of processing by lower production of consumer goods, clothing and shoes. It said that the seasonally-adjusted figure, which takes into account the number of working days in the period, was identical to the monthly figure of -3.9 percent.

The average nominal industrial wage in January was 9,904 crowns compared with 10,461 in December. The January index of real wages was up 6.5 percent. The real wage index was 7.9 percent higher for the whole of 1996.
Wage results sample companies with 100 or more employees while output results include estimates of smaller firms as well.

The CSU said that construction output was greatly influenced by poor weather conditions this winter, which cut the average number of working hours by some 10.6 percent, year-on-year. The year-on-year figure was also influenced by a rush of construction in January 1996 on the Ingolstadt oil pipeline.
